claims.text: The initial CrB-based boride coating has inherent surface porosity and microdefects.
An aluminum-rich alloy can be reactively infiltrated into defects in the CrB-based coating.
The infiltration should be performed in argon at approximately 650°C.
Approximately 650°C is high enough to promote reactive wetting of the aluminum-rich alloy on the boride coating.
Approximately 650°C is below the full melting point of aluminum.
Reaction between the aluminum-rich infiltrant and the boride surface will produce a continuous, dense intermetallic layer.
The proposed intermetallic layer may be an Al3X-type phase containing a refractory element derived from the boride.
The intermetallic reaction layer will fill surface porosity and seal corrosion pathways.
A compact barrier layer can hinder diffusion and reduce further chemical attack.
The proposed intermetallic layer will be thermodynamically stable in contact with molten aluminum.
The barrier will reduce exposure of vulnerable CrB-based coating phases to molten aluminum.
Reactive infiltration will reduce the molten-aluminum corrosion rate relative to an untreated CrB-based coating.
The treatment will improve molten-aluminum corrosion resistance by roughly 35% relative to untreated controls.
The improvement will be observable as reduced weight loss and slower corrosion-front propagation.
Protection will remain effective when infiltration is performed in argon near 650°C.
Significantly higher processing temperatures or incomplete infiltration may compromise barrier formation.
The magnitude of improvement may depend on infiltration uniformity, infiltrant composition, and processing reproducibility.
Failure to achieve at least a 35% reduction in weight loss or corrosion-front penetration relative to untreated controls would falsify the hypothesis.
Failure to detect the intended intermetallic layer would falsify the hypothesis.
